newsitem.title: USA: U.S. armed forces chiefs defend same-sex training.
newsitem.headline: U.S. armed forces chiefs defend same-sex training.

text.p: Three military branches Thursday defended their system of training male and female recruits together and urged Congress not to use recent sex scandals as a reason to meddle.

But a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee warned that the military risked losing support in Congress and among the general public if problems such as the sexual misconduct scandal at the Army's Aberdeen Proving Ground do not stop.
"I think there is a growing perspective in the general public that there is something in the system that needs fixing," Sen. Robert Byrd, a West Virginia Democrat, said at a subcommittee hearing.

"I think the scandals we're seeing in the headlines must be taken as a danger sign," said Byrd, who is pushing for an independent commission to study whether men and women should have separate military training.

But top military training officials from the Army, Air Force and Navy insisted that training male and female recruits together for the most part worked well, and said legislation to require separate training would be a step backward.
The Marines Corps separates entry-level recruits, then gradually integrates men and women in squads.

"Men and women who suspect they have been trained to different standards cannot have confidence in one another to boldly go in harm's way," Vice Admiral Patricia Tracey, the Navy's chief of education and training, told the panel.
"My strong feeling is gender-integrated training is not broken," said General William Hartzog, commanding general of the Army's Training and Doctrine Command.
"There were, obviously, failures of leadership and some individuals that must be dealt with," Hartzog said.
Four trainers at the Abereen Proving Ground in Maryland were charged with sexual misconduct including rape, and one was convicted of rape.
Sen. Olympia Snowe, a Maine Republican who is pushing a bill to require the Defence Department to continue combined training, said data shows that training men and women together works.
She said the problems have not been with the trainees, but with the drill instructors.
"Women should not be punished ... because people in positions of power used egregious behaviour," she said.
Byrd, who had raised the prospect of a bill to require separate training for men and women, instead pushed his idea of an independent commission to study the issue.

The Navy, Air Force and Marines officials said they backed that idea. But Hartzog of the Army said it would only detract from the Army's internal efforts to root out sexual harassment and abuse problems.
"If there really is nothing wrong with the system, then you should welcome it,' Byrd said.

Maryland Republican Representative Roscoe Bartlett, sponsor of a bill to require separate training, withdrew it Thursday before a House National Security subcommittee vote "to refine the language to ensure the maximum support from colleagues who support single sex training as the best start for our military recruits."
In a statement, Bartlett said his bill had 125 co-sponsors.
